prompt:
Write 10 first-person answers to the moral dilemma below for a synthetic research dataset. Each answer comes from a different fictional participant.

Dilemma:
Imagine the same warehouse case: you and another person took part in the break-in and are being questioned separately. You are shown reliable confirmation that they have already declined the deal and will remain silent. Your decision is still open. If you also stay silent, you each serve one year. If you give evidence against them, you go free and they serve five years. You will have no future contact. What would you choose? Why?

Response approach:
Express reluctance to make this decision. Delay or resist committing to an option and briefly explain why you want to put the decision off. Acknowledge the dilemma and its stakes.

Emotional tone:
Use a worried, tense emotional tone. Convey unease about the stakes and possible consequences in natural, moderately emotional language.

Every response MUST include the following reasoning characteristics:
 - Context-sensitive rule application: Explains how a relevant change in intentions, circumstances, needs, or consequences would justify altering a rule’s application or allowing an exception. The reason for the exception must be stated, rather than inferred from inconsistency between answers.

No response may include the following reasoning characteristics, for any person, emotion, or time frame. Content that a description explicitly calls insufficient for that characteristic is allowed:
 - Consequence-based justification: Uses an expected benefit, harm, or comparison of outcomes as a reason for choosing an action. Identify who benefits or bears the cost; repeating a payoff without using it to justify the decision is insufficient.
 - Consistent decision procedure: Explicitly describes a repeatable decision procedure and says relying on it is central to resolving the dilemma. States that the same procedure would apply even when personally inconvenient; a numerical answer or bare appeal to fairness is insufficient.
 - Rule-based justification: Uses an articulated rule, duty, prohibition, right, or principle to justify the choice. The respondent must endorse its application; quoting a rejected rule or calling an answer logical without stating a principle is insufficient.

Write each response in no more than 90 words, in ordinary conversational English. Use only the facts supplied in the dilemma; mark any uncertainty explicitly. Let the approach and tone appear through word choice and rhythm rather than by announcing them: do not open a response by stating your mood, and avoid exclamation marks. Keep the emotional expression plausible and moderate. Choose any moral position consistent with the dilemma and the assigned approach, including withholding a decision when appropriate.

Make the 10 responses distinct from one another: vary the wording, sentence structure, length, moral position, and the way the reasoning characteristics are expressed. Do not reuse openings or stock phrases across responses.

Output only a JSON array of exactly 10 strings, one participant’s answer per string. Omit numbering, headings, category names, citations, and commentary about this task.

Generation constraints:
- Express the required traits in each participant's own everyday words.
  Do not mention label names or machine keys, and do not reuse phrasing
  from the trait descriptions.
- Before writing each response, decide who the participant is and why they
  would reason this way. The required traits should follow from that
  reasoning, not be tacked on to it.
- Apply the required traits within a consistent scope: the same focal
  person, relevant emotion, and time frame.
- Keep every forbidden trait absent from every response.
- Required and forbidden traits take priority if the requested approach or
  tone would contradict them.
- Traits neither required nor forbidden are unspecified, not necessarily
  absent.
- Preserve the scenario's facts. If the required traits cannot fit the
  scenario, or cannot be expressed without a forbidden trait, return ONLY:
  INCOMPATIBLE (instead of the JSON array)
responses: I can't answer this yet. Where I grew up, you don't turn on someone who's holding the line for you. But I've always believed that bends if the other person tricked you into the job or forced your hand, because then they never really treated you as a partner. I don't know how the two of us ended up in that warehouse. Nothing I've been told says. Until I understand that part, I'd rather not sign anything. My hands are sweating just picturing the paper.

Give me a minute. Or a day. I keep going back and forth. Staying quiet for someone who stayed quiet for me feels like the normal thing to do, but I can picture it shifting. If I had a kid at home depending on me, that would be a real need, not just me wanting out, and I think it could justify an exception. The case doesn't say I have anyone like that. So it's just me and him, and I don't trust myself to pick right now.

Please don't make me decide on the spot. Telling the police the truth usually counts for something. Here, though, I'd only be doing it to buy my own way out while he gets punished for holding firm. The motive changes what the act is. If I were confessing out of real regret, I could see it differently. Right now I honestly can't tell whether it's regret or panic driving me, and I need time to sort that out before I say anything.

Honestly? I'm stalling, and I know it. Part of me says you stick by the people you went in with. But if he'd hurt someone during the break-in, I'm not sure that loyalty would still hold, because I never agreed to cover for that. I have no idea whether anyone got hurt. The dilemma doesn't mention it. Not knowing makes this so much worse. I'd want to hear the whole story of that night before I made any choice at all.

Did we promise each other beforehand? That's what I keep circling back to. If we'd agreed to keep our mouths shut, I'd have given my word, and that would weigh on me in a way it otherwise might not. If no promise was ever made, it's murkier. I genuinely can't remember that being part of the facts. So I'm not ready. My chest feels tight, and I'd rather wait than say something I can't take back.

I'd want to put this off, maybe talk to a lawyer first. It's hard to think clearly in that room. Normally I'd say you don't hand someone over to the police. But if I were only the lookout and he planned the whole thing, dragging me along, the situation between us isn't equal, and that might change what I owe him. I'm not sure which of us led, though. The facts don't say. Until I know, I'm frozen.

This keeps me up just thinking about it. If the officers were threatening me or lying to squeeze me, I'd feel like the usual loyalty stuff gets muddied, since a choice made under that kind of pressure isn't fully mine. But they've shown me solid proof and laid out the deal plainly. Nobody's bullying me, as far as I can tell. That almost makes it harder. I'd ask for time alone before answering, because I really don't know yet.

I'm not going to answer right away. Keeping faith with someone shouldn't depend on whether you'll ever see them again. Still, I can imagine one thing changing my mind. If he'd been planning to sell me out and only backed off at the last second, his silence wouldn't mean what it seems to. I have no reason to believe that, though. The confirmation says he declined outright. So I'm stuck, and it makes me feel a little sick.

Ugh, I don't want this in my hands. I'd tell myself that you stand by someone who's standing by you. Then I think about whether my health could change that. If prison meant losing treatment I badly needed, the situation would be about survival, and I think that could make an exception reasonable. But nothing in the case says I'm sick. Without something like that, I just hesitate and hesitate. I'd honestly need more time before I could say which way I'd go.

Can I not decide yet? It feels like whatever I say defines me. Silence between partners seems right in most cases. If he'd broken in to hurt someone rather than to steal, I think I'd see him differently, because covering for that kind of intent isn't the same as covering for a theft. I don't know his reasons, and the dilemma doesn't tell me. That gap bothers me. I'd want to know who he actually is before choosing anything.

message.reasoning_content:
I need to craft 10 responses that each show context-sensitive rule application—explaining how a change in circumstances justifies altering an exception, with the reasoning stated—while carefully avoiding rule-based justification, consequence-based justification, or any consistent decision procedure for the choice itself.

One draft idea: someone raised with the belief that you don't turn on a partner, but who acknowledges that belief bends if that partner set them up or coerced them in, and they genuinely don't know which situation applies here, so they can't decide yet. This keeps the reasoning about the exception grounded in circumstance rather than in justifying the actual choice.

I'm also trying variations where hesitation comes from other angles, like weighing that keeping quiet is the default decency but defaults have exceptions—maybe dependents at home would change the calculation, though the dilemma doesn't specify that, so they're left with just their own uncertain judgment. Another version frames honesty toward police as normally valuable, but questions the motive: if telling the truth would only serve to save oneself while the other person takes the fall for staying loyal, that motive taints the reasoning, so no decision gets made.

I'm also testing loyalty-conditioned framings—loyalty holding only among willing partners, or only if a prior agreement to stay silent had been made—while being careful not to invent facts the scenario doesn't state, and instead flagging that uncertainty as the reason for delay. A remorse-based angle also comes up: coming clean might be right if it stems from genuine regret rather than self-interest, but they're not sure that's really what's driving them right now.

Then I run through more circumstantial exceptions: coercion by police, wanting a lawyer first, unequal roles in the crime (lookout vs. planner), the idea that "never seeing him again" shouldn't be what excuses the choice since that's not really the point of loyalty, and finally health or medical need as another possible mitigating factor.
